title: Energy
scope: Choose the objectives in your school’s topic list. These are original practice questions with illustrative values, not a claim of an official school paper format.

objectives.label: Explain and use energy conservation.
objectives.note: Energy is conserved when transfers across the chosen system boundary are fully counted.

objectives.label: Explain and use kinetic energy.
objectives.note: For the low-speed classical model, kinetic energy is half mass times speed squared.

objectives.label: Describe stores and transfers, calculate mechanical work and gravitational potential energy changes.
objectives.note: An energy store describes a system’s state; a transfer describes how energy moves between stores or systems.

objectives.label: Explain and use efficiency.
objectives.note: Efficiency compares useful output energy or power with total input energy or power.

objectives.label: Explain and use power.
objectives.note: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy transferred divided by elapsed time.

objectives.label: Explain and use electricity generation.
objectives.note: Generators transfer energy from other sources; energy supplies differ in availability and environmental consequences.

cards.definition: Energy is conserved when transfers across the chosen system boundary are fully counted.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A pupil claims a frictionless machine can deliver energy forever without any decrease in its source or input. Explain the problem. Useful output energy must come from an input or a decrease in an energy store. Producing a continuing output with neither would violate energy conservation.
cards.confusion: Energy spreading into surroundings is not energy being destroyed.
cards.question: Explain energy conservation from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Energy is conserved when transfers across the chosen system boundary are fully counted. Energy spreading into surroundings is not energy being destroyed.

cards.definition: For the low-speed classical model, kinetic energy is half mass times speed squared.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Two identical model trolleys move at 3 m/s and 6 m/s. Compare their kinetic energies and explain why doubling speed does not merely double this energy. Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared for fixed mass. The energy ratio is 6²/3² = 4. The faster trolley therefore has four times the kinetic energy.
cards.confusion: Doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, not by two.
cards.question: Explain kinetic energy from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: For the low-speed classical model, kinetic energy is half mass times speed squared. Doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four, not by two.

cards.definition: An energy store describes a system’s state; a transfer describes how energy moves between stores or systems.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A battery drives a motor that lifts a mass. Identify an initial and a final energy store. The battery’s chemical store decreases. The gravitational potential store of the Earth–mass system increases, with some energy transferred to surroundings.
cards.confusion: Heating is a transfer process, not a substance held in an object.
cards.question: Explain stores and transfers from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: An energy store describes a system’s state; a transfer describes how energy moves between stores or systems. Heating is a transfer process, not a substance held in an object.

cards.definition: Efficiency compares useful output energy or power with total input energy or power.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A model motor has efficiency 30% and must provide 210 J of useful output. Calculate the required input energy. Efficiency as a fraction = 0.30 = useful output ÷ input. Input = 210 ÷ 0.30 = 700 J.
cards.confusion: An inefficient device still conserves total energy when all outputs are counted.
cards.question: Explain efficiency from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Efficiency compares useful output energy or power with total input energy or power. An inefficient device still conserves total energy when all outputs are counted.
cards.formula: efficiency = useful output / total input; multiply by 100 for %

cards.definition: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy transferred divided by elapsed time.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A 45 W model device must transfer 675 J at constant power. Calculate the time required. Time = energy transferred ÷ power. 675 ÷ 45 = 15 s.
cards.confusion: Power and energy have different units.
cards.question: Explain power from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy transferred divided by elapsed time. Power and energy have different units.

cards.definition: Generators transfer energy from other sources; energy supplies differ in availability and environmental consequences.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: Give one reason a city cannot assume a solar panel supplies its rated power continuously throughout every day. Sunlight varies with time and weather and is absent at night, so rated power is not supplied continuously.
cards.confusion: Renewable does not mean there are no environmental effects.
cards.question: Explain electricity generation from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Generators transfer energy from other sources; energy supplies differ in availability and environmental consequences. Renewable does not mean there are no environmental effects.

cards.definition: A force does work when there is displacement with a component along that force.
cards.explanation: A force does work when there is displacement with a component along that force.
cards.example: A 10 N force acting along a 2 m displacement does 20 J of work.
cards.confusion: A force can act without doing work if the displacement is perpendicular to it.
cards.question: Explain mechanical work from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: A force does work when there is displacement with a component along that force. A force can act without doing work if the displacement is perpendicular to it.
cards.formula: W = Fd for a constant force parallel to displacement

cards.definition: Near a surface with approximately constant g, the increase in gravitational potential energy is mg times the vertical height gained.
cards.explanation: Near a surface with approximately constant g, the increase in gravitational potential energy is mg times the vertical height gained.
cards.example: Raising the same load twice as far gives twice the potential-energy increase.
cards.confusion: Use vertical height change, not the length of a sloping path.
cards.question: Explain gravitational potential energy from memory and give its important distinction.
cards.answer: Near a surface with approximately constant g, the increase in gravitational potential energy is mg times the vertical height gained. Use vertical height change, not the length of a sloping path.
